summary: The future is the present (the imperfect) with سَـ joined to it or the separate word سَوْفَ before it: أُسَافِرُ “I travel” → سَأُسَافِرُ / سَوْفَ أُسَافِرُ “I will travel”. The person prefix stays: سَأُسَافِرُ, سَتُسَافِرُ, سَيُسَافِرُ, سَنُسَافِرُ. سَـ is the everyday form; سَوْفَ is a word of its own and often sounds more distant or more emphatic. A plan with a time word may also stay in the present: أَزُورُ الْجِيرَانَ غَدًا “I’m visiting the neighbours tomorrow”. The future is negated with لَنْ + the subjunctive (the present with -a): لَنْ أُسَافِرَ “I will not travel” — لَنْ takes the place of سَـ / سَوْفَ. Questions put هَلْ or a question word in front: هَلْ سَتَحْجِزِينَ غُرْفَةً؟ — أَيْنَ سَتَذْهَبُونَ؟. Time words for the future: غَدًا, الْأُسْبُوعَ الْقَادِمَ, السَّنَةَ الْقَادِمَةَ, قَرِيبًا, بَعْدَ سَاعَةٍ.

blocks.caption: سَافَرَ “to travel”: the future is سَـ + the present; the negative is لَنْ + the subjunctive.

blocks.title: سَـ + present = future.
blocks.text: Nothing else changes: the prefix and the ending of the present stay (سَأَزُورُ، سَتَزُورِينَ، سَيَزُورُونَ). سَوْفَ works the same way as a separate word: سَوْفَ نَحْجِزُ غُرْفَةً.

blocks.title: لَنْ + subjunctive.
blocks.text: The subjunctive changes -u to -a (أُسَافِرُ → لَنْ أُسَافِرَ), drops the -na of -īna / -ūna (تُسَافِرِينَ → لَنْ تُسَافِرِي، يُسَافِرُونَ → لَنْ يُسَافِرُوا, with a silent alif) and keeps the -na of the feminine plural (لَنْ يُسَافِرْنَ). Verbs in -ā do not change: لَنْ أَنْسَى.

items.title: سَـ
points: joined to the verb; the everyday future, near or general

items.title: سَوْفَ
points: a separate word; often further away in time or more emphatic

blocks.title: The present can be enough.
blocks.text: With a time word the plain present often says the future: أُسَافِرُ غَدًا “I’m travelling tomorrow”, أَزُورُ الْجِيرَانَ غَدًا. سَـ makes the future explicit.

head: Arabic
meaning
blocks.caption: Time words for the future. الْقَادِم “coming” agrees with its noun: الْأُسْبُوعَ الْقَادِمَ but السَّنَةَ الْقَادِمَةَ.

blocks.title: No سَـ with a negation.
blocks.text: Not *سَلَا أُسَافِرُ, not *لَا سَأُسَافِرُ: “I will not travel” is لَنْ أُسَافِرَ. لَا أُسَافِرُ is “I don’t travel / I’m not travelling”.

blocks.title: “Will be”: سَيَكُونُ.
blocks.text: The future of كَانَ is سَيَكُونُ / سَتَكُونُ, and like كَانَ it puts its predicate in the accusative: سَتَكُونُ الرِّحْلَةُ طَوِيلَةً “the trip will be long”.

askYourself: Is it a plan, a promise or a prediction for later? → سَـ + present (or سَوْفَ + present).
Who? Keep the person prefix of the present: سَأَـ (I), سَتَـ (you / she), سَيَـ (he / they), سَنَـ (we).
Is the time already clear from a word like غَدًا? → the plain present is also possible.
Negative? → لَنْ + subjunctive: drop سَـ / سَوْفَ, -u → -a (لَنْ أُسَافِرَ), -īna / -ūna lose -na.
A question? → هَلْ or a question word before the future verb: هَلْ سَتُسَافِرُ؟ / مَتَى سَتَعُودُ؟

traps: سَـ is written joined to the verb: سَأُسَافِرُ, never *سَ أُسَافِرُ.
The negation is لَنْ, not لَا: لَنْ أَنْسَى “I won’t forget”; لَا أَنْسَى is “I don’t forget”.
After لَنْ the verb ends in -a: لَنْ نَحْجِزَ, not *لَنْ نَحْجِزُ.
لَنْ تُسَافِرُوا: -ūna loses -na and an alif is written (تُسَافِرُونَ → تُسَافِرُوا).
سَـ never goes before a past verb: *سَسَافَرْتُ is impossible.

quiz.why: The future is negated with لَنْ + subjunctive; لَمْ أَنْسَ is “I didn’t forget”.
After لَنْ, -ūna loses -na: يَحْجِزُوا (with a silent alif).

quiz.answer: as a separate word before the verb
quiz.why: سَوْفَ أَزُورُ; the short form سَـ is the one written joined: سَأَزُورُ.

options: I used to visit the neighbours.
quiz.why: With a time word the present can speak about the future.

seeAlso.note: In Hebrew the prefix conjugation itself is the future (אֶסַּע “I will travel”); in Arabic the same kind of form is the present, and سَـ makes it future (سَأُسَافِرُ).
German has werden + infinitive (ich werde reisen) but often uses the present with a time word (ich reise morgen) — exactly like أُسَافِرُ غَدًا.
Chinese puts 要 / 会 / 打算 before an unchanged verb; Arabic joins سَـ to a verb that already carries the person.
The future is built on the present: سَـ + أُسَافِرُ; its negation uses the subjunctive, which also follows أَنْ “to” (أُرِيدُ أَنْ أُسَافِرَ).

notes.text: Greek forms the future with θα + verb (θα ταξιδέψω); Arabic’s سَـ is similar but written joined to the verb, and the negation changes the particle: لَنْ أُسَافِرَ (Greek keeps θα: δεν θα ταξιδέψω).
Russian has a one-word future of perfective verbs (поеду) and буду + infinitive (буду ездить); Arabic always builds the future from the present with سَـ / سَوْفَ.
Spanish has a one-word future (viajaré) and ir a + infinitive; Arabic’s present for plans (أُسَافِرُ غَدًا) matches “viajo mañana”, and سَأُسَافِرُ the future tense.
“will” is a separate word like سَوْفَ; Arabic usually joins its short form سَـ to the verb, and “won’t” is another particle, لَنْ, with a changed verb ending (لَنْ أُسَافِرَ).
French has a one-word future (je voyagerai) and aller + infinitive (je vais voyager); Arabic builds it from the present with سَـ / سَوْفَ and negates it with لَنْ.
German uses werden + infinitive or simply the present with a time word (ich reise morgen); Arabic does both: سَأُسَافِرُ or أُسَافِرُ غَدًا.
Hindi has a one-word future that shows the speaker’s gender (मैं जाऊँगा / जाऊँगी); the Arabic future is the present with سَـ, and its “I” form has no gender (سَأَذْهَبُ).
Persian builds the written future with خواستن + the short past stem (خواهم رفت “I will go”) and in speech uses the present (می‌روم), as Arabic can (أَذْهَبُ غَدًا).
Marathi has a future ending (मी जाईन “I will go”); Arabic adds the prefix سَـ to the present (سَأَذْهَبُ).
Hebrew’s future is the prefix conjugation (אֶסַּע “I will travel”), the twin of the Arabic present; Arabic needs سَـ to make that form future (سَأُسَافِرُ).
Turkish has a future suffix (gideceğim “I will go”); Arabic puts a particle in front of the present (سَأَذْهَبُ).
Japanese has no future form: the non-past (行く) covers it, as the Arabic present can (أَذْهَبُ غَدًا); Arabic adds سَـ when the future is meant explicitly.
Korean uses -(으)ㄹ 거예요 for plans and predictions (갈 거예요 “I will go”); Arabic uses سَـ + present (سَأَذْهَبُ).
Finnish has no future tense: the present with a time word does the job (matkustan huomenna); Arabic can do the same (أُسَافِرُ غَدًا) or add سَـ.
Hungarian uses the present for the future (holnap utazom) or fog + infinitive; Arabic uses the present or سَـ + present.
Swahili marks the future with -ta- inside the verb (nitasafiri “I will travel” — the verb itself comes from Arabic سَافَرَ); Arabic puts سَـ in front of the present (سَأُسَافِرُ).
Luganda distinguishes a near and a remote future in the verb; Arabic has one future, سَـ / سَوْفَ + present, and shows distance with time words.
Chinese uses 要, 会 or 打算 before an unchanged verb (我要去埃及); Arabic joins سَـ to a verb that already carries the person (سَأُسَافِرُ).
Vietnamese puts sẽ before the verb (tôi sẽ đi), a separate word like سَوْفَ; but the Vietnamese verb does not change, while the Arabic verb carries the person (سَأَذْهَبُ / سَنَذْهَبُ).
Inuktitut marks the future with a suffix inside the verb word (-langa-); Arabic puts سَـ before the present.
